title: Checks on the Courts
short: The other branches check the courts by appointing and confirming judges, passing new laws after a statutory ruling, proposing amendments, setting the courts' size and some of their jurisdiction, and by how they carry out rulings; the courts have no army or budget of their own.
trouble: Students think a Supreme Court ruling on a statute can only be undone by a constitutional amendment. If the ruling interprets a statute, Congress can simply amend the statute.

blocks.html: Hamilton called the judiciary "the least dangerous" branch, since it has "neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment" and depends on the executive to carry out its rulings (Federalist No. 78). Along with appointments, the other branches hold several more checks on the courts.

blocks.html: Why so many checks on unelected judges? Courts protect rights even against majorities, but in a democracy their power still answers, slowly, to the people: through the officials who choose judges, the laws Congress writes, and amendments. Which tool fits depends on what the Court decided. If it read a statute, Congress can simply change the statute. If it read the Constitution, only an amendment, or a later Court, can change the result.

Courts are checked by appointments, new laws after statutory rulings, constitutional amendments, Congress's control of courts' size and jurisdiction, impeachment, and their reliance on others to enforce rulings.

blocks.title: Statute or Constitution?
blocks.q: The Court rules that a federal law's word "employee" does not cover interns. Congress disagrees. What can it do?
steps: The Court interpreted a statute, not the Constitution.
Congress can pass a new law saying "employee" includes interns.
blocks.a: Amend the statute by ordinary law.

blocks.title: Overturning a constitutional ruling
blocks.q: In Oregon v. Mitchell (1970) the Court held that Congress could not set an 18-year-old voting age for state elections. How was that changed?
steps: The ruling read the Constitution, so a statute could not undo it.
Congress proposed the Twenty-sixth Amendment, and the states ratified it in 1971.

blocks.html: Thinking a Supreme Court ruling can only be undone by a constitutional amendment. That is true when the Court reads the Constitution. When it reads a statute, Congress can amend the statute, as it did after Ledbetter. Check: what text was the Court interpreting?
